```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(powershift)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

brand <- c(
  ink = "#222222",
  muted = "#B8B8B8",
  accent = "#006DAE"
)

focus_colours <- c("Context" = brand[["muted"]], "Focus" = brand[["accent"]])
line_colours <- c("Context" = "grey48", "Focus" = brand[["accent"]])

theme_cwd <- function(base_size = 16) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
      axis.title = element_text(colour = brand[["ink"]]),
      axis.text = element_text(colour = brand[["ink"]]),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = brand[["ink"]]),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey35"),
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", hjust = 0),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      plot.margin = margin(10, 36, 10, 10)
    )
}
```

This guide is for an **energy policy analyst preparing a briefing on a
country's electricity transition**. It shows how to install powershift,
launch and use its app, and read the results to answer one question:

> How much has a country's electricity from one source changed between two
> years, and was that faster or slower than in other countries?

## Shares and percentage points

A source's **share** is the percentage of a country's electricity generated
from it in a year. The **change** between two years is measured in
**percentage points**: the end-year share minus the start-year share. If
coal's share falls from 79% to 43%, that is a fall of 36 points. Because the
shares of all sources add up to 100% each year, a fall in one source is
matched by rises in others.

## Install the package

```{r}
#| eval: false
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-tambatsmit")
```

## Launch the app

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(powershift)
run_app()
```

The app uses the `electricity_mix` data included in the package, so it needs
no other files.

## Use the app

Work down the sidebar:

1. **Country to focus on:** the country you are briefing on. It is drawn in
   blue and summarised in the three boxes.
2. **Countries to compare with:** the countries to set it against, drawn in
   grey. Click in the box and type a name to add a country; click a name and
   press Delete to remove it.
3. **Source of electricity:** the source whose share you want to follow, such
   as coal or solar.
4. **Years to compare:** drag either end of the slider to set the start and
   end years.

The page then shows:

- **Three boxes:** the focus country's share in the end year, its change in
  percentage points, and how many of the countries shown have data for both
  years.
- **Compare countries tab:** a headline answering the question for the focus
  country, a sentence giving the range of changes across the countries shown,
  and a chart of each country's share over the years chosen.
- **Whole mix tab:** the change in every source's share for the focus
  country, which shows what replaced what.
- **Table tab:** each country's share in both years, the change, the change
  per year and the result in words.
- **Guide tab:** what each control and field means, and the limitations.

## Read the outputs

The app's first view follows coal in Australia from 2005 to 2025, compared
with the United Kingdom, Germany, the United States, China and India.
`share_change()` produces the same numbers:

```{r}
countries <- c(
  "Australia", "United Kingdom", "Germany", "United States", "China", "India"
)

changes <- share_change(electricity_mix, from = 2005, to = 2025)

coal <- changes |>
  filter(source == "coal", country %in% countries) |>
  arrange(change)

coal |>
  select(country, from_share, to_share, change, change_per_year)
```

Coal's share of Australia's electricity fell by
`r round(-coal$change[coal$country == "Australia"], 1)` points, the largest fall
of these countries, but in 2025 coal still supplied
`r round(coal$to_share[coal$country == "Australia"], 1)`% of its electricity.
The United Kingdom's share fell by a similar amount from a lower start, to
almost nothing, and India's share rose. The `result` column is the text the
app shows in its headline and table:

```{r}
coal$result[coal$country == "Australia"]
```

The app's chart shows the same comparison:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Line chart of the share of electricity from coal from 2005 to 2025 for
#|   six countries. Australia is drawn in blue and falls from about 79% to
#|   43%. The United Kingdom falls to almost zero and India stays near 70%.
plot_data <- electricity_mix |>
  filter(
    source == "coal",
    country %in% countries,
    between(year, 2005, 2025)
  ) |>
  mutate(focus = if_else(country == "Australia", "Focus", "Context"))

endpoints <- plot_data |>
  group_by(country) |>
  slice_max(year, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

ends <- plot_data |>
  filter(year %in% c(2005, 2025))

ggplot(plot_data, aes(year, share, group = country)) +
  geom_line(colour = brand[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.75) +
  geom_line(
    data = filter(plot_data, focus == "Focus"),
    colour = brand[["accent"]],
    linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  geom_point(data = ends, aes(colour = focus), size = 3) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = endpoints,
    aes(label = country, colour = focus),
    direction = "y",
    hjust = 0,
    nudge_x = 0.4,
    segment.colour = NA,
    seed = 5523
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = line_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = scales::breaks_width(5),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.22))
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of electricity from coal") +
  theme_cwd(base_size = 13)
```

How to read it:

- Each line is one country. The **dots** mark the start and end years.
- The vertical gap between a country's two dots is its change in percentage
  points. A **steeper line** means faster change.
- The focus country is **blue**; the countries it is compared with are grey.

## What replaced coal

The Whole mix tab uses the same function to show the change in every source
for the focus country:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Bar chart of the change in each source's share of Australia's
#|   electricity from 2005 to 2025. Coal fell by about 37 points, while
#|   solar rose by about 20 points and wind by about 13 points.
mix <- changes |>
  filter(country == "Australia", !is.na(change)) |>
  arrange(change) |>
  mutate(
    source = factor(source, levels = source),
    focus = if_else(source == "coal", "Focus", "Context")
  )

ggplot(mix, aes(change, source, fill = focus)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = brand[["ink"]]) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = round(change, 1),
      hjust = if_else(change < 0, 1.15, -0.15)
    ),
    colour = brand[["ink"]]
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = focus_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.15)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    x = "Change in share of electricity, 2005 to 2025 (percentage points)",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_cwd(base_size = 13)
```

Solar (`r round(mix$change[mix$source == "solar"], 1)` points) and wind
(`r round(mix$change[mix$source == "wind"], 1)` points) together made up most
of coal's fall, with gas filling some of the rest.

## When a change cannot be measured

Some countries have no change for a source, and the app says why:

```{r}
changes |>
  filter(
    country %in% c("Indonesia", "Australia"),
    source %in% c("coal", "nuclear"),
    is.na(change)
  ) |>
  select(country, source, result)
```

- **No data for a year:** Indonesia's figures end in 2024, so the app reports
  "No data" and asks you to move the slider to years with data. Australia's
  nuclear figures also end in 2024; they are zero in every year reported.
- **No data at all:** some countries never report a source. Australia has no
  "other renewables" figures, so the app asks you to choose another source or
  country.
- **The same start and end year:** the app asks you to choose two different
  years.

If no comparison countries are chosen, or none of them has data for both
years, the app asks you to add countries or choose other years.

## Limitations

**Shares are not amounts.** A falling share can hide rising use, because the
share also depends on how much electricity a country generates in total. The
`generation` column shows the amount, in terawatt-hours (TWh):

```{r}
china <- electricity_mix |>
  filter(country == "China", source == "coal", year %in% c(2005, 2025)) |>
  select(year, generation, share)

china
```

China's coal share fell, but its electricity from coal rose from
`r format(round(china$generation[1]), big.mark = ",")` TWh to
`r format(round(china$generation[2]), big.mark = ",")` TWh, almost three times
as much.

**Electricity is only part of energy.** Cars, heating and industry also burn
fossil fuels directly, and they are not counted here.

**Coverage varies.** Only about 80 of the 213 countries have data before
2000, and the 2025 figures are early estimates for about 90 countries, which
may be revised.

## Data source

Our World in Data energy dataset,
<https://github.com/owid/energy-data>, based on Ember's Yearly Electricity
Data and the Energy Institute's Statistical Review of World Energy, licensed
under CC BY 4.0. `data-raw/electricity_mix.R` prepares the data, and
`?electricity_mix` describes every column.
